messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar was 22 when he came for help, a single Middle Eastern American man working as an auditor, and he described himself as someone who had once moved through the world with ease. Before the assault, he had taken pride in being composed at work, careful in how he presented himself, and comfortable enough in public to meet clients, sit in conference rooms, and move between unfamiliar buildings without much thought. That changed after he was raped. He did not dwell on the details at length in the first sessions, but when he described the event, it was with a tightness that made clear how vividly it remained with him: the violation had been intimate, coercive, and degrading, leaving him not only frightened in the moment but later overwhelmed by the sense that something in him had been permanently exposed. What stayed with him most was the humiliation. He said he felt as if he had been marked by it, as though the event had stripped away a version of himself he had assumed was solid and private.

In the weeks and months that followed, Omar noticed that ordinary experiences began to carry a charge they had never held before. Certain smells could pull him back into the memory without warning, especially related smells that seemed to arrive all at once and make his stomach tighten before he could even identify them. He also found himself bracing when he encountered people behaving badly in public, especially if they were being intrusive, disrespectful, or dismissive in a way that seemed to mirror the moral violation of what had happened to him. Even casual remarks could be difficult if they sounded like relationship reminders; if someone said things like “my ex,” he would feel a jolt of recognition and discomfort, as though the conversation had brushed against a part of his life he was trying not to touch. These moments were not dramatic from the outside, but they were intensely personal for him, and he reported that they could leave him unsettled for hours.

Omar had also developed a set of habits that shaped his days. At work, he made sure to stay near an exit whenever he could, choosing seats at the edge of meeting rooms and positioning himself so he would not feel trapped if he needed to leave quickly. As an auditor, he often had to enter unfamiliar offices, walk through buildings he did not know well, and sit in rooms where other people were watching and assessing him. Those situations had become especially difficult. He avoided unfamiliar places when he could because he could not assess the danger in them, and the uncertainty itself felt intolerable. He was also increasingly wary of situations in which other people evaluated him, his appearance, or his performance. He worried about being scrutinized, about being judged before he could steady himself, and he began choosing concealing clothing so he would not be noticed. He described this as a way of making himself less visible, less available to anyone’s attention, and more able to get through the day without feeling exposed.

At the same time, his body seemed to remain on duty even when nothing obvious was happening. He described being constantly tense and ready to react to danger, as if his muscles had forgotten how to soften. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard; if a coworker turned quickly behind him or someone stepped toward him unexpectedly, he would stiffen before he could think. He was aware of scanning spaces, measuring distances, and noticing where people were standing, especially in places he had not been before. The alertness gave him a sense of being prepared, but it also left him exhausted, and he said it was hard to remember the last time he had fully relaxed.

The meanings he had made of the assault were harsh and enduring. Omar repeatedly compared himself to other men and was certain that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation. He spoke about it with a mix of shame and disbelief, as though the fact that it happened to him said something permanent about his judgment or his worth. He also said, with palpable sadness, that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable. That was not how he had expected his early twenties to feel, and the contrast between who he had been and how he felt now seemed to trouble him deeply. More than anything, he felt permanently humiliated by what happened, and that humiliation made social situations feel charged and vulnerable.

By the time he sought treatment, these changes had narrowed his life in practical ways. He was still working, but the effort of managing meetings, rooms, and public interactions had become taxing, and he noticed how much energy he spent choosing clothes, choosing seats, and choosing routes. He came in because he was tired of feeling as though every day required him to brace against some new threat, and because the shame had become harder to carry alone. What he most wanted was to feel like himself again, or at least to believe that the humiliation and vigilance would not define the rest of his life.
